analysis.one_liner: Caps pain-and-suffering awards in federally backed health care lawsuits and makes medical lawsuits harder to bring.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 218-210 on June 28, 2017, but the Senate never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules for medical malpractice lawsuits in any case where the patient's care was paid for by a federal program, subsidy, or tax benefit — which covers most insured care, since employer health insurance gets a federal tax break. It would cap compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000, set shorter deadlines for suing, cap lawyers' contingency fees, require a signed expert affidavit before filing, restrict who can testify as an expert witness, and bar patients from naming a doctor or pharmacist in a product liability lawsuit over an FDA-approved drug or device. The House passed it mostly along party lines; the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and the insurers who write their malpractice policies gain the most, because the bill lowers the amounts they must pay when care goes wrong. Drug and device makers also gain from the damage caps and shorter filing deadlines, though the bill bars naming prescribing providers alongside them in product suits. The bill's stated aim is to reduce 'defensive medicine' costs that supporters said were driving up premiums and health spending.

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic damages — compensation for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and loss of enjoyment of life — at $250,000 per injury, no matter how many parties or claims are involved, while leaving compensation for actual monetary losses like medical bills and lost wages unlimited.
Cuts the time patients have to sue to three years after the injury or one year after discovering it, whichever comes first, unless there was fraud, concealment, or a foreign object left in the body.
Caps plaintiffs' attorney contingency fees on a sliding scale, from 40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% of anything over $600,000, and lets courts supervise how awards are paid out.
Bars patients from naming a health care provider as a defendant in a product liability or class action lawsuit over an FDA-approved drug, device, or biological product they prescribed or dispensed.

Requires a sworn expert affidavit supporting the case before a lawsuit can be filed, restricts expert witnesses to professionals licensed and practicing in the defendant's state or a bordering state, and makes providers' apologies and expressions of sympathy inadmissible as evidence.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical negligence lose the most: their pain-and-suffering compensation is capped at $250,000 regardless of how severe or permanent the harm, juries are not told the cap exists and awards above it are silently cut, filing deadlines are shorter, and new pre-filing requirements raise the cost and difficulty of bringing a case. Patients hurt by an FDA-approved drug or device can no longer sue the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed it alongside the manufacturer.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap applies no matter how catastrophic the injury — a patient left brain-damaged or disabled for life by negligence would collect the same maximum pain-and-suffering award as someone with a minor injury, and the jury is never told the cap exists.
The bill reaches nearly all insured patients, because it covers any care paid for through a federal program, subsidy, or tax benefit, and employer health coverage receives a federal tax benefit.
Critics in the House argued during the floor debate on the motion to recommit that the bill should exempt negligent opioid prescribing, and that motion failed on a party-line vote of 191-235.
The pre-filing affidavit, expert-witness residency rules, and 90-day advance notice requirements add cost and delay for patients with legitimate claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argue unlimited malpractice awards drive up insurance premiums and push doctors toward wasteful defensive medicine, and that capping damages lowers costs. The cost falls on a specific group: patients catastrophically injured by negligent care, whose largest category of compensation would be capped and whose path to court would be narrower. Economic damages stay unlimited, but for injuries whose main harm is pain and lost quality of life, the cap is the whole case. Whether lower premiums would materialize for patients was not established by anything in the record.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 218-210 on June 28, 2017, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never took it up, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill on March 22, 2017, by an 18-17 vote after a February 28 markup, and the Energy and Commerce Committee was discharged the same day.

On June 28, 2017, the House rejected a Democratic motion to recommit that would have added an exemption for negligent opioid prescribing, 191-235, with all voting Democrats in favor and all voting Republicans against.
The House passed the bill 218-210: 218 of 241 voting Republicans in favor, 19 Republicans voting no, and all 193 voting Democrats opposed.
The Senate received the bill on June 29, 2017, and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients and the plaintiffs' attorneys who represent them keep the existing malpractice rules, since the Senate never took up the bill. Doctors, hospitals, and their malpractice insurers did not get the lower liability exposure the bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients keeping current lawsuit rights

industries.note: The bill caps the payouts insurers must make for pain and suffering and limits attorney fees, directly shrinking their claims exposure. The cost is borne by injured patients whose compensation would have come from those claims.

Caps on damages, shorter filing deadlines, expert-witness restrictions, and pre-filing requirements all reduce malpractice liability for providers. Supporters argued lower liability costs would reduce premiums and defensive medicine, but the direct effect is that patients wronged by negligent care collect less.

industries.industry: Drug, device, and biological product makers
industries.note: Manufacturers gain from the $250,000 damage cap and shorter deadlines in suits over federally covered care, but Section 6 bars naming prescribing providers in product liability suits, leaving manufacturers as the remaining defendants and removing a defense based on prescriber fault.

Sliding-scale caps on contingency fees, mandatory expert affidavits, and tight expert-witness qualifications would shrink the volume and economics of malpractice practice. Because these lawyers are paid out of patients' recoveries, their loss tracks directly with the reduced compensation patients would receive.
